h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Fort Worth
intro: Fort Worth investors work with a housing stock that is older and more varied than the city's cowboy image suggests. Fairmount and Ryan Place hold some of the densest collections of early twentieth-century bungalows in Texas. The Northside and Diamond Hill have small frame houses built for families who worked the Stockyards and packing plants. The east side, from Polytechnic Heights to Stop Six, is full of mid-century homes that need systems and structure, and the southwest has postwar ranches in Wedgwood and the areas around it. Genstone Construction coordinates vetted, licensed contractors across Fort Worth for investors, lenders and servicers, managed by our estimators and field managers from headquarters in Romeoville, Illinois. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the repairs and tests your ARV before you commit capital, and every project runs on a detailed scope, a draw schedule tied to finished work and one field manager from start to finish.
housingStock:
Fort Worth's older housing is concentrated in a ring around downtown, and its character changes sharply by direction.

South of downtown, Fairmount, Ryan Place, Mistletoe Heights, Berkeley Place and the Near Southside were built from roughly the 1900s through the 1920s. Craftsman bungalows dominate, with Prairie, foursquare and some Tudor and Colonial Revival houses mixed in. These homes sit on pier-and-beam foundations, usually with wood siding, deep porches, original wood windows and tongue-and-groove or oak floors. Many have been partially updated over the decades, leaving a mix of old and new wiring, galvanized and copper supply lines and cast-iron drains.

West of downtown, Arlington Heights, Monticello and Ridglea filled in from the 1920s through the 1940s with bungalows, Tudor cottages and brick traditionals, many on pier-and-beam and some on early slabs. The Northside and Diamond Hill have smaller frame houses from the same period, often expanded with rear additions.

East of downtown, Polytechnic Heights near Texas Wesleyan University and neighborhoods like Riverside, Oakhurst and Meadowbrook include a mix of early frame houses and postwar ranches. Stop Six, Como and parts of the southeast were built out largely in the 1940s through the 1960s with modest frame and brick homes. In the southwest, Wedgwood and nearby subdivisions have brick slab ranches from the 1950s and 1960s.

Farther out, the north side around Alliance and the far southwest have newer tract construction that trades as suburban product. Near TCU, the streets of Bluebonnet Hills, University West and Frisco Heights hold small 1930s through 1950s houses and duplexes, many of them long since converted to student rentals and worn accordingly. For investors, the older ring matters most, and its common thread is foundation movement in clay soils, original systems that have outlived their design life and wood exteriors that have seen decades of Texas sun.

commonIssues.title: Pier-and-beam settlement
commonIssues.body: Most of Fort Worth's prewar housing sits on pier-and-beam foundations, and decades of clay movement leave floors that slope toward the perimeter, interior doors that bind and cracks in plaster or drywall. Some houses still sit on original cedar posts or short concrete piers that have tilted or sunk. Leveling, adding piers, replacing rotted sills and sistering damaged joists is routine work in Fairmount, Arlington Heights and the Northside, and it should be done before finish work begins.

commonIssues.title: Hail and wind damage
commonIssues.body: Fort Worth sits in one of the most hail-prone parts of the country, and the city has a long history of damaging storms, including the 1995 Mayfest hailstorm and the 2000 downtown tornado. Roofs, gutters, siding, window screens and HVAC condenser fins all take damage. On an investor purchase, we check roof age, look for bruised shingles and dented metal, and review any claim history the seller can provide, then price repair or replacement before listing.

commonIssues.title: Slab movement and drain lines
commonIssues.body: Postwar brick ranches in Wedgwood, the east side and the southeast often sit on slabs placed directly on expansive clay. Seasonal swelling and shrinking crack the slab, the brick veneer and the cast-iron drain lines underneath. A leaking drain under a slab can saturate the soil and worsen movement. We recommend a camera inspection and, where cracks or slopes are present, a foundation evaluation before you finalize your offer.

commonIssues.title: Old wiring and undersized service
commonIssues.body: Prewar houses in Fairmount and Arlington Heights may still have knob-and-tube or cloth-sheathed wiring in walls and attics, often spliced into later circuits. Postwar homes may have small panels or brands that insurers and inspectors flag, and some homes from the 1960s and early 1970s contain aluminum branch wiring. We trace circuits, recommend service and panel upgrades where needed, and make sure everything passes city electrical inspection.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and wood exterior repair
commonIssues.body: Wood siding, trim and windows on Fort Worth's older homes almost always carry layers of lead-based paint, and renovation that disturbs them must follow lead-safe practices. After years of sun and rain, siding and trim also develop rot, especially at the bottom courses and around windows. We budget for lead-safe prep, wood repair or replacement with matching profiles, and a durable paint system, which matters in historic districts where original materials are expected.

investorMarket:
Fort Worth investors tend to sort themselves by direction from downtown.

South of downtown, Fairmount, Ryan Place, Mistletoe Heights and the Near Southside are retail flip territory. Buyers pay for restored bungalows with updated kitchens, baths and systems, and the Magnolia Avenue corridor has drawn restaurants and small businesses that support demand. Historic district rules apply in much of this area, which shapes exterior scope.

West of downtown, Arlington Heights and Ridglea support both flips and higher-end rentals, with buyers drawn to the Cultural District and proximity to West 7th. Near TCU, neighborhoods like Bluebonnet Hills, University West and Frisco Heights have a strong student and young professional rental market, with duplexes and small houses that rent by the bedroom.

The Northside and Diamond Hill offer smaller houses at lower price points, often with additions and deferred maintenance. They suit buy-and-hold and BRRRR investors, and some areas near the Stockyards have seen rising interest. The east side, including Polytechnic Heights, Riverside, Stop Six and Meadowbrook, has a mix of rental investors, REO activity and early-stage reinvestment, where scopes center on foundation, roof and systems.

In the southwest, Wedgwood and nearby areas have brick ranches that fit long-term rental strategies, with steady demand from families and workers across the region. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps sort out which strategy fits a specific house, because conditions and comps can change quickly from one block to the next.
permits:
Residential permits in Fort Worth are issued by the City of Fort Worth Development Services Department. Foundation repair, structural changes, plumbing, electrical and mechanical work, re-roofing, window replacement that alters openings and additions require permits and inspections. Licensed trades, through the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners and the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, must pull plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.

Fort Worth has an active historic preservation program. Properties in local historic districts, including Fairmount, Ryan Place and Mistletoe Heights, and individually designated landmarks need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic and Cultural Landmarks Commission or staff for exterior changes such as window replacement, siding, porch modifications, roofing material changes and additions. Some minor work can be approved administratively. Unapproved work can result in required corrections.

Fort Worth Code Compliance enforces minimum building standards on occupied and vacant properties. Addresses in suburban cities such as Arlington, Haltom City, Benbrook and White Settlement, or in unincorporated Tarrant County, fall under their own permitting offices. Before any Fort Worth scope is final, our estimators verify which office has the address and whether a historic overlay applies.
climate:
Fort Worth weather is hard on houses in three ways. Summers are long and hot, which dries out clay soils and causes foundation movement, especially on the east side. Spring brings hail, high winds and occasional tornadoes that can damage roofs, siding and windows across large parts of the city in a single afternoon. Winters are usually mild, but ice storms and hard freezes, including Winter Storm Uri in 2021, burst pipes in attics, exterior walls and crawlspaces.

These patterns shape scheduling. Foundation leveling is often best done when soils are neither saturated nor extremely dry. Roofing crews get booked out after major hailstorms, so scheduling roof replacements before storm season is helpful. Exterior painting and concrete work are planned around summer heat. For crawlspace houses, we include pipe insulation and skirting repairs to reduce freeze risk.

faqs.q: Do you work in Arlington, Haltom City and other Tarrant County cities?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate licensed contractors across Tarrant County, including Arlington, Haltom City, Benbrook, White Settlement, Richland Hills, Saginaw, North Richland Hills and Burleson. Each city has its own building department and inspection process, and some have their own rental or code programs. We confirm local requirements for each address before scoping, so the permit plan fits the city the house is actually in.

faqs.q: How do historic district rules affect a Fairmount renovation?
faqs.a: In Fairmount, Ryan Place, Mistletoe Heights and other local historic districts, exterior changes like window replacement, siding, porch work, roofing materials and additions generally need a Certificate of Appropriateness. Interior work is usually not reviewed. We check district status during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and design exterior work to meet the guidelines, which often means repairing original wood windows and siding rather than replacing them.

faqs.q: How do you handle foundation repair on a Fort Worth house?
faqs.a: We bring in a licensed foundation contractor and, where the condition warrants, a structural engineer to evaluate and document the repair. On pier-and-beam homes, that usually means leveling, adding or replacing piers and repairing sills and joists. On slab homes, it may mean installing piers. Foundation work is scheduled first so later finishes are not damaged, and reports and warranties go into your sale or refinance package.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay anything upfront?
faqs.a: No. Nothing is due before work starts. Each draw follows a finished, photographed stage of the job, and the last payment waits until the house is complete and you have signed off. Haul-off and dumpsters are already priced into the estimate. Our work carries a one-year workmanship warranty that excludes tenant damage and normal wear, and our billing team keeps lien waivers and contractor compliance records organized.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fort Worth fix and flip renovations for Fairmount, Arlington Heights and Ridglea buyers: pier leveling, restored details, hail-ready roofs and fast draws.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Fort Worth
fix-flip.intro: The strongest Fort Worth flips tend to come from the bungalow belt south and west of downtown. Fairmount, Ryan Place, Mistletoe Heights, Arlington Heights and Ridglea draw buyers who want an older home with real character, close to Magnolia Avenue, the Cultural District or TCU, and they will pay for one that has been restored properly. Brick ranches in Wedgwood and the southwest can also flip well when the foundation, roof and kitchen are handled correctly. Genstone builds flip scopes around what Fort Worth buyers and their inspectors care about. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work, checks historic district status and refines your ARV before you commit, and our field manager coordinates licensed local contractors through permits, approvals and finish work so the house reaches the market with documentation buyers trust.

sections.body:
A Fairmount or Ryan Place bungalow sells on its porch, its windows and its woodwork. Buyers there want tapered porch columns, original or matching wood windows, built-ins, original floors and trim intact, with a kitchen and baths that work for modern life. Flips that strip out character in favor of a generic interior tend to sit longer and sell for less.

Our scopes for these houses begin with the foundation. Leveling the pier-and-beam structure, replacing rotted sills and correcting sagging joists comes first, followed by rewiring to remove old knob-and-tube or cloth-sheathed circuits, replacing galvanized and cast-iron plumbing, and adding central air with ductwork routed through the attic or crawlspace. Exterior work focuses on wood siding and trim repair with matching profiles, window restoration or approved replacement, and lead-safe paint preparation. Inside, we refinish original floors where possible, keep or recreate period trim and doors, and design kitchens and baths that fit the house. We price multiple finish levels so you can match what recent sales on your street actually support.

sections.h2: Arlington Heights, Ridglea and Wedgwood buyers
sections.body:
West of downtown, Arlington Heights and Ridglea attract buyers who want character close to the Cultural District and West 7th, but these neighborhoods are less uniform than Fairmount. You will find bungalows, Tudor cottages, brick traditionals and some postwar houses on the same streets. Buyers here expect quality kitchens and baths, updated systems and well-kept exteriors. Many of these homes are not in historic districts, which gives more flexibility on windows and exterior materials.

In Wedgwood and the southwest, the flip is a brick ranch competing against other updated ranches. Buyers value open kitchen layouts, updated baths, durable flooring and efficient systems, and their inspectors focus on the roof, slab, drains, electrical panel and HVAC. Our scope for these houses typically includes a camera inspection of drain lines, a foundation evaluation where cracks or slopes appear, roof assessment for hail damage and age, panel upgrades where needed and properly sized HVAC. Visible spend goes where buyers notice it most: kitchens, baths, flooring and curb appeal.

sections.h2: Approvals, permits and staying on schedule
sections.body:
Flip profits depend on carrying costs, and in Fort Worth approvals can be as important as construction speed. In Fairmount, Ryan Place and other historic districts, exterior work may need a Certificate of Appropriateness before it starts. We identify those items early and submit promptly, then sequence interior work so crews keep moving while approvals are pending.

Permits for foundation, plumbing, electrical, HVAC and roofing go through the City of Fort Worth Development Services Department, and inspections must pass in sequence. Our field manager schedules inspections and coordinates trades to minimize downtime. Weather matters too: spring hail and storms can delay roofing, and summer heat slows exterior painting and concrete work. Because draws are tied to completed work and progress is documented with milestone photos, you can track the schedule without visiting the site and share updates with lenders or partners. On older houses we also order long-lead items, such as custom-profile siding, matching trim or restored window sashes, as soon as the scope is final, because waiting on a millwork shop is a common and avoidable cause of delay in the historic neighborhoods.

faqs.q: Should I replace the windows in a Fairmount bungalow?
faqs.a: In the Fairmount historic district, replacing original wood windows on visible elevations generally requires approval and a product that matches the original design. Restoration of original windows is often the expected path and can be a selling point. If windows are beyond repair, we can prepare an approved replacement option. We price both so you can weigh the cost against the schedule and what buyers on that street reward.

faqs.q: How much foundation work does a typical Fort Worth flip need?
faqs.a: It varies widely. Some pier-and-beam houses need only minor leveling and shimming, while others need new piers, sill replacement and joist repair. Slab ranches may need piers installed along a settling section. We evaluate the foundation during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and include a licensed foundation contractor's assessment where warranted, so the cost is known before you buy. The engineer's letter and foundation warranty then become part of your listing package.

faqs.q: Will hail damage affect my Fort Worth flip?
faqs.a: If the roof has hail damage or is near the end of its life, the buyer's inspector will flag it, and the buyer's insurer may require replacement. That usually leads to a price reduction or repair request. We assess roof condition during scoping and price replacement when warranted, so you can decide whether to handle it before listing. A new roof also photographs well and answers a question buyers ask early.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Fort Worth BRRRR rehabs on Northside, Polytechnic and Wedgwood houses: foundation, roof and systems fixed for the refi appraisal with tenant-proof finishes.
brrrr.intro: Fort Worth BRRRR deals usually come from the Northside, Diamond Hill, Polytechnic Heights, Riverside and the brick ranch neighborhoods of the southwest and southeast, where purchase prices leave room for a full rehab and rental demand is steady from families and workers across Tarrant County. The renovation has to support a refinance appraisal and then hold up to tenants for years. In Fort Worth, that means addressing foundation movement, hail-worn roofs and aging systems before spending on finishes. Genstone scopes BRRRR projects with both goals in mind. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and ARV before you buy, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans if you want to plan the refinance alongside the renovation. One field manager coordinates licensed local contractors, permits and inspections, with documented progress at each draw.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Fort Worth refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Fort Worth appraisers compare your property to nearby sales and adjust for condition and usable square footage. Houses on the Northside and in Diamond Hill often have rear additions or enclosed porches built over many years, and unpermitted space may not count in the appraisal. We evaluate each addition and price both legalization and removal, so your projected ARV reflects what the appraiser will see.

Systems and visible condition are the other major drivers. A house with a level foundation, a sound roof, updated electrical and plumbing and reliable HVAC appraises better than one with new finishes over old systems. We target finishes at the level comparable rentals and sales support, usually durable vinyl plank, mid-range counters and updated fixtures, and invest the rest in the items an appraiser and underwriter will look at. Foundation reports, permit records and roof documentation are organized so you can answer questions quickly during the refinance.

sections.h2: Built for tenants and North Texas weather
sections.body:
A Fort Worth rental needs to handle hot summers, hailstorms and occasional hard freezes. We size HVAC systems properly, seal ductwork and add attic insulation where it is thin, which reduces cooling bills and tenant complaints. On pier-and-beam houses, exposed plumbing in the crawlspace is insulated and skirting is repaired to protect against freezes. Roofs are inspected for hail damage and replaced when warranted, because an aging roof is a source of leaks and insurance issues.

Inside, we use waterproof vinyl plank, semi-gloss paint in kitchens and baths, solid cabinets and standard fixtures that are easy to replace. Outside, we pay attention to gutters, downspouts and grading so water drains away from the foundation, which reduces seasonal movement. On wood-sided houses, we repair rot and use durable paint systems. These choices lower turnover costs and help the property hold value for future refinancing or sale. On Northside and Diamond Hill houses with rear additions, we also check where the addition roof ties into the main roof, because that joint is a frequent leak point after heavy storms.

sections.h2: Where BRRRR fits in Fort Worth
sections.body:
The Northside, Diamond Hill and Polytechnic Heights offer smaller frame houses with lower purchase prices and scopes that usually include foundation leveling, electrical and plumbing updates and decisions about additions. Riverside and parts of the east side have a mix of frame and brick homes with similar needs. In the southwest and southeast, brick ranches in Wedgwood and nearby areas tend to have simpler scopes centered on roof, HVAC, drains and interior updates.

We are cautious about houses in historic districts for BRRRR, since restoration-level exterior work raises costs without always raising rents. We also check for severe foundation movement and flood exposure near the Trinity River and creeks. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we evaluate these factors and give you a realistic scope and ARV, so you can see whether the property will support a refinance before you buy. We also note the rental drivers in each area, such as access to the Alliance logistics corridor for north-side houses, or proximity to downtown, the hospital district and the Stockyards for close-in homes, since those shape how quickly a finished rental leases.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial refinance my Fort Worth BRRRR?
faqs.a: That is one option. Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, provides DSCR rental loans as well as fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. A DSCR loan qualifies based on the property's rental income, which works well for many BRRRR investors. Using Genstone Financial is optional, and we provide the same scope, draw documentation, foundation reports and completion records to any lender you choose, so your Fort Worth refinance can move as soon as the house is leased.

faqs.q: What about unpermitted additions on Northside houses?
faqs.a: Many Northside and Diamond Hill houses have additions built without permits. If the addition is sound, permitting it after any needed corrections can add appraised square footage. If it is poorly built, removal may be the better option. We evaluate and price both so your BRRRR numbers reflect the right choice. The roof tie-in and foundation under the addition are usually where problems hide.

faqs.q: How do you protect rentals from freeze damage?
faqs.a: On pier-and-beam houses, we insulate exposed plumbing, repair skirting and seal openings in the crawlspace. On slab homes, we check pipes in exterior walls and attics. These steps reduce the risk of burst pipes during hard freezes like Winter Storm Uri, when many Fort Worth crawlspace homes lost supply lines. We also make sure tenants know where the main shutoff is, which limits the damage if a pipe does split.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Fort Worth single-family rental renovations: Wedgwood ranches, east-side frame homes and Alliance-area tract houses held to one durable portfolio standard.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in Fort Worth
rental-renovation.intro: Fort Worth rental portfolios tend to straddle two kinds of housing. Close to downtown, owners hold frame houses on the Northside, in Polytechnic Heights and across the east side, most of them pier-and-beam and most of them older than anyone living in them. Farther out, they hold brick ranches in Wedgwood and the southeast and newer tract homes toward Alliance, Saginaw and Benbrook. A good rental program treats those houses differently while keeping one standard for finishes, pricing and reporting. Genstone works with landlords, funds and institutional owners to renovate and turn single-family rentals across Fort Worth and Tarrant County. We coordinate licensed local contractors, assign one field manager per property and document every draw. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps acquisitions teams price houses before they buy, using the same scope format the renovation team will follow.

sections.h2: One standard, three kinds of Fort Worth house
sections.body:
Every Fort Worth rental we renovate starts from the same baseline: waterproof vinyl plank, a single paint family, standard cabinet sizes and fixtures available at any supply house, sealed ductwork, correctly sized HVAC, working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and secure locks. What changes is where the money goes beyond that baseline.

On prewar frame houses near downtown, it goes underneath and into the walls. Floors are leveled, piers and sills repaired, crawlspace plumbing insulated, and old wiring removed. Wood siding and trim are repaired and repainted with lead-safe preparation. On postwar brick ranches in Wedgwood and the southeast, the focus shifts to roofs that have taken hail, slabs that have moved, cast-iron drains under the slab and original electrical panels. On newer tract homes toward Alliance and Saginaw, the work is usually lighter, centered on HVAC equipment reaching the end of its life, water heaters, builder-grade fixtures and flooring. Keeping that distinction clear stops the portfolio from overspending on easy houses and underspending on difficult ones, and it gives asset managers a realistic picture of capital needs house by house.

sections.h2: Covering Tarrant County under one program
sections.body:
A Fort Worth portfolio rarely stays inside city limits. Owners commonly hold houses in Haltom City, Richland Hills, White Settlement, Benbrook, Saginaw and North Richland Hills alongside their Fort Worth addresses, plus some in unincorporated Tarrant County. Each city has its own permit office, its own inspectors and, in some cases, its own approach to rental property standards. Newer subdivisions add homeowners association rules on exterior colors, fences and roofing materials.

Genstone handles that spread with one written scope standard and one reporting format, while our licensed, insured contractor network does the local work. Each property gets a field manager responsible for permits, inspections, lien waivers and contractor compliance in the correct jurisdiction, and for checking HOA requirements where they apply. Asset managers see milestone photos and draw requests without driving across the county. Our estimators flag houses that need capital work beyond a turn, such as a pier-and-beam house that has settled since acquisition or a ranch with a roof at the end of its life, so annual budgets track the real condition of the portfolio rather than an assumed average.

sections.h2: Turns timed to hail season and summer heat
sections.body:
Fort Worth's weather gives rental turns a natural calendar. Late winter and early spring are the best time to service or replace HVAC equipment, before the first heat wave fills every contractor's schedule with emergency calls. Late spring and early summer, after the worst of hail season, are the right time to inspect roofs, gutters, screens and condensers for storm damage and to file claims where appropriate. Fall is the time to check crawlspace skirting, pipe insulation and hose bibs on older houses before the first freeze.

We scope each turn to catch predictable failures rather than just repaint and clean. That includes checking water heater age and pressure relief valves, clearing condensate lines, re-caulking tubs and showers, replacing worn weatherstripping and logging any new drywall cracks that suggest foundation movement. Genstone Field Services also provides occupied maintenance, inspections and code compliance between tenancies, so one organization can handle renovation and upkeep. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work we perform and excludes tenant damage and normal wear, and each turn is documented for your records and any future sale.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals outside Fort Worth city limits?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across Tarrant County, including Haltom City, Richland Hills, White Settlement, Benbrook, Saginaw, North Richland Hills, Burleson and unincorporated areas. Each city has its own permit office and inspection process, and newer subdivisions often have HOA exterior rules. We confirm requirements for each address, then apply your portfolio standard so quality and reporting stay consistent wherever the house sits.

faqs.q: How do you handle older pier-and-beam rentals?
faqs.a: We coordinate licensed foundation contractors to level floors, replace or add piers and repair sills and joists, and we insulate crawlspace plumbing and repair skirting to reduce freeze risk. Doing that work during a vacancy is far easier than scheduling it around a tenant, and it heads off the door, drywall and plumbing calls that follow when a house keeps settling.

faqs.q: Can you keep costs consistent across a large portfolio?
faqs.a: Yes. We work from a written finish and systems standard that you approve and use the same line-item estimate format for every property. That makes houses easy to compare and spending easy to track. We only depart from the standard where a property's age or condition requires it, and we explain each departure in the scope so there are no surprises at billing.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & Fourplex Renovation in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Fort Worth 2–4 unit renovations: TCU-area duplexes, Fairmount garage apartments and east-side brick fourplexes, phased around tenants with shared systems fixed.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Small Multifamily Renovations in Fort Worth
multifamily-renovation.intro: Fort Worth's small multifamily buildings cluster in a few places. Around TCU, in Bluebonnet Hills, University West and Frisco Heights, you find duplexes and small houses that rent to students and young professionals, often by the bedroom. Fairmount and the Near Southside have older houses split into units and garage apartments behind main houses, many inside historic districts. On the east and southwest sides, brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1950s through the 1970s house working families. Each type brings different shared systems, code questions and tenant expectations. Genstone helps investors renovate 2–4 unit buildings across Fort Worth by coordinating licensed local contractors, phasing work around tenants and managing permits and historic approvals. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work before you buy so you can test it against current and projected rents.

sections.body:
Near TCU, small duplexes and houses converted to multiple units are common, and they take hard use. Student tenants are rough on flooring, doors, bathrooms and kitchens, and many of these buildings have been patched rather than renovated over the years. Typical problems include undersized electrical service for the number of occupants, shared water heaters that cannot keep up, worn-out bathroom plumbing, failing window air conditioners or tired central systems, and pier-and-beam floors that have settled.

Our scopes for these buildings prioritize durability and simplicity. We upgrade electrical service and separate circuits where needed, give each unit its own water heater when feasible, replace plumbing and fixtures with commercial-grade options that stand up to heavy use, and install properly sized HVAC. Flooring is waterproof and easy to replace, paint is scrubbable, and hardware is standard. We also check bedroom egress windows and smoke alarms carefully, because buildings rented by the room need every sleeping space to meet code. The goal is a building that turns quickly every summer and generates fewer calls during the school year.

In Fairmount and the Near Southside, many larger houses were divided into two or more units decades ago, and garage apartments behind main houses are common. These buildings come with the same issues as the area's bungalows, such as pier-and-beam settlement, old wiring and plumbing and lead paint, plus multifamily-specific concerns like shared utilities and limited fire separation between units.

Before scoping, we review the building's history and confirm whether the number of units is legal under current zoning. Many of these properties are legal nonconforming uses, which generally allows continued use but may limit changes. Exterior work in the Fairmount historic district requires approval from the Historic and Cultural Landmarks Commission or staff, including stairs, porches, windows and additions. Our scopes typically include foundation leveling, electrical service upgrades and separate metering where practical, plumbing replacement, improved fire separation and smoke detection and HVAC that suits each unit. We plan exterior work to meet the district guidelines from the start.

sections.h2: Phasing occupied buildings on the east and southwest sides
sections.body:
Brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1950s through the 1970s on the east and southwest sides of Fort Worth usually come with tenants in place. These buildings have slabs on clay that move, single-pane windows, aging HVAC and plumbing, and roofs that may have hail damage. Shared drain lines under the slab are often cast iron nearing the end of its life.

We phase work so vacant units are renovated first, then occupied units are completed as leases end or tenants move into finished units. Shared-system work such as a main drain replacement or electrical service upgrade is scheduled with written notice and short shutoffs. In summer, HVAC work in occupied units is done quickly or deferred to cooler months. Our field manager coordinates access, keeps common areas safe and documents progress, and Genstone Field Services can handle occupied maintenance in units not yet renovated, keeping the building in good order throughout the project.

faqs.q: Can I rent a TCU-area duplex by the bedroom?
faqs.a: Many investors do, but it depends on zoning and occupancy rules that limit the number of unrelated occupants in some districts. Each bedroom also needs to meet egress and smoke alarm requirements. We recommend confirming occupancy limits with the city before you plan your rent roll around per-bedroom leases, and we scope the building so every sleeping room meets code.

faqs.q: Is a Fairmount garage apartment a legal unit?
faqs.a: It depends on when and how it was built, current zoning and whether it was ever permitted. Some are legal nonconforming units, while others were added informally. We review records and physical conditions and explain what it would take to bring the unit into compliance, including any exterior work that needs historic district approval. Separate utilities, a proper exterior stair and egress from the sleeping room are the items that most often come up.

faqs.q: Can an east-side Fort Worth fourplex stay occupied during the rehab?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Empty units get finished first and become the move-in option for tenants in the units that come next, and the rest are completed as leases roll over. Anything that cuts water, power or sewer to the whole building is posted in writing ahead of time. Our field manager is the single point of contact for tenants and trades. On a slab fourplex, replacing a shared cast-iron drain is the most disruptive step, so we plan it for a single, well-announced window and have the plumber ready to restore service the same day.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor in Fort Worth: pier leveling, rewiring, hail roofs and historic-district repairs bid for Limited or Standard 203(k) loans.
fha-203k.intro: Fort Worth has a lot of houses that sit just outside conventional financing: a Polytechnic Heights bungalow with sloping floors, a Wedgwood ranch with a hail-worn roof and an original panel, a Northside cottage with old wiring and a failing addition. An FHA 203(k) loan lets a buyer finance the purchase and the repairs together, with the work done after closing under a structured draw process. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and we work with buyers, agents, lenders and HUD consultants across Fort Worth to prepare the detailed bids and draw schedules the program requires. We coordinate licensed local contractors, manage permits and historic approvals where needed, and keep everyone informed through each draw. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps buyers understand repair costs before they write an offer.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard on a Fort Worth home
sections.body:
Non-structural work up to $75,000 can go through the Limited 203(k), and no HUD consultant is required. In Fort Worth, that version fits houses with a stable foundation that need practical updates: a roof replacement after hail, new HVAC, a panel upgrade, insulated windows, flooring, paint and kitchen or bath work. Many brick ranches in Wedgwood and the southwest and southeast fit this description once the slab checks out.

The Standard 203(k) is required when the project includes structural repairs, and in Fort Worth that most often means foundation work. Leveling a pier-and-beam bungalow in Fairmount or Polytechnic Heights, installing piers under a settling slab, or rebuilding a failing rear addition on a Northside cottage all fall into Standard territory. Standard loans need at least $5,000 of eligible repairs, and a HUD consultant inspects the house, writes up the work and signs off on each draw. Our team meets that consultant at the first walkthrough so our bid matches the write-up and so foundation work is scheduled ahead of drywall, tile and paint.

sections.h2: Fort Worth houses that make good 203(k) candidates
sections.body:
The best candidates are houses in neighborhoods buyers want, priced down by problems that are obvious and fixable. A bungalow in Fairmount or Ryan Place that needs leveling, rewiring, new plumbing and a kitchen is a classic Standard project and can put a buyer into a neighborhood that would otherwise be out of reach. A 1950s or 1960s ranch in Wedgwood with a roof at the end of its life, old HVAC and a dated kitchen is a classic Limited project.

Fort Worth adds a few local cautions. In historic districts like Fairmount and Ryan Place, exterior repairs such as window replacement or porch rebuilding may need a Certificate of Appropriateness, which adds a step and affects the schedule. Rear additions and enclosed porches built without permits are common on the Northside and east side, and they may need to be legalized or removed for the loan to close. Nearly all of these houses predate 1978, so lead-safe practices apply whenever paint is disturbed. We flag these issues in the early estimate so buyers, agents and lenders can plan around them.

sections.h2: Bids, draws and documentation for Fort Worth lenders
sections.body:
Fort Worth 203(k) loans stall most often on documentation, not construction. Lenders want each repair priced separately with labor and materials shown, and on a Standard loan the numbers have to tie out to the consultant's write-up. Once the loan closes, the repair money sits in escrow and comes out in stages after each round of work is inspected. Past the $15,000 threshold, the inspection and paperwork requirements increase.

Our estimators write bids in the layout Fort Worth lenders and consultants are used to reviewing, and the field manager calls for each draw inspection as soon as a stage is finished. We do not require upfront payment, and our draws are tied to finished work, which aligns with how the program releases funds. Permits are pulled through the City of Fort Worth Development Services Department, and historic approvals are requested early where needed. Inspection sign-offs and photos go out with each draw request. Many 203(k) buyers are paying rent while the work happens, so we order long-lead items such as HVAC equipment, windows and custom millwork as soon as the loan closes to keep the move-in date realistic.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover foundation leveling in Fort Worth?
faqs.a: Yes, through the Standard 203(k). Leveling counts as structural repair, which rules out the Limited loan. We coordinate with the HUD consultant, a licensed foundation contractor and, where needed, a structural engineer to scope, price and document the repair. Leveling is scheduled first so later finishes are not damaged, and the buyer keeps the engineer's letter and any warranty for future resale.

faqs.q: Does a historic district complicate a 203(k) in Fairmount?
faqs.a: It adds a step. Exterior repairs in Fairmount and other local historic districts may need approval before work begins, which affects the schedule and sometimes the choice of materials. Interior work is generally not reviewed. We check district status early, design exterior work to meet the guidelines and submit for approval promptly. Interior trades keep working while the application is reviewed, so the approval step rarely holds up the whole job.

faqs.q: Do you work with Fort Worth agents and loan officers?
faqs.a: Yes. Tarrant County buyers' agents frequently call us while a house is still under option, so their client can see what the foundation, roof and wiring will really cost. Once the buyer commits, we write the line-item bid for the lender, meet the HUD consultant on site for Standard loans and send each party the same draw updates, photos and inspection sign-offs until the work is complete.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Fort Worth, TX | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Fort Worth REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: settled pier-and-beam homes, hail roofs, freeze damage, vandalism and code compliance, all documented.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Fort Worth
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned homes in Fort Worth tend to decline along the same lines. Older pier-and-beam houses on the Northside, east side and south of downtown settle further once nobody is watching, and their crawlspace plumbing is exposed to every hard freeze. Brick ranches lose roofs to hail and condensers to thieves. Vacant lots grow tall grass and draw code complaints. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, which use us as a preferred contractor, to stabilize and renovate REO properties across Fort Worth and Tarrant County. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, while our construction team handles repairs. We coordinate licensed local contractors, document conditions and progress at every step, and help each asset reach the disposition that makes the most sense.

sections.h2: Conditions common in vacant Fort Worth homes
sections.body:
Freeze damage is one of the most frequent findings in Fort Worth REO properties, particularly older pier-and-beam houses where supply lines run through an open crawlspace. Winter Storm Uri in 2021 split pipes in many vacant homes across the city, and some were not discovered until the water had soaked subfloors, framing and insulation. Roof damage from hail and wind is close behind. A roof that took a storm during foreclosure may have leaked for months, leaving stained or collapsed ceilings, wet insulation and mold in attic and wall cavities.

Foundation movement also accelerates when a house sits empty through a dry summer with no watering, and both pier-and-beam and slab homes show new cracks in brick, drywall and floors. Theft and vandalism are common, including stolen AC condensers, water heaters, appliances and copper. On older wood-sided homes, deferred maintenance shows as rotted siding, failing porches and broken windows. Our initial inspection documents each condition with photos and a preliminary scope so servicers can decide quickly between repair and as-is disposition.

sections.h2: Stabilize, repair and prepare for sale
sections.body:
Fort Worth REO projects typically move through three phases. Stabilization comes first: securing doors and windows, winterizing plumbing, tarping roofs, removing debris and personal property and addressing immediate hazards like exposed wiring. Our Field Services crews usually carry out that first phase. Repairs follow and focus on items that affect value or financing, usually roof replacement, foundation leveling or piering, plumbing and electrical repairs and replacing stolen or failed HVAC equipment. Listing preparation comes last, with paint, flooring, cleaning, lawn care and curb appeal.

For most Fort Worth assets we price at least two paths. One is a light scope for selling as-is to investors. The other brings the house up to the minimum property requirements that FHA and VA appraisers check, which widens the buyer pool to owner-occupants. Seeing both side by side lets asset managers judge which path is likely to net more. In historic districts like Fairmount, exterior repairs are planned to meet guidelines so the property does not stall on approvals. Debris removal is included in every estimate, and draws are tied to completed, documented work with milestone reports that let asset managers follow progress remotely.

Fort Worth Code Compliance enforces minimum standards on vacant properties, including high grass and weeds, open or unsecured structures, accumulated trash and unsafe conditions. Violations can lead to citations, city abatement charges and liens that complicate disposition. Genstone Field Services monitors properties on a schedule, keeps lawns maintained through the growing season and responds to notices quickly so violations do not pile up while the asset is being marketed.

When repair work begins, permits go through the City of Fort Worth Development Services Department or the relevant suburban building department for addresses in Arlington, Haltom City, White Settlement and other Tarrant County cities. Foundation, roofing, electrical and plumbing work each need permits and inspections, and we keep the sign-offs in the project file. Exterior work on properties in local historic districts is submitted for approval before it starts. Lien waivers and contractor compliance documents are collected on every job and organized for audit, so servicers and investors have a complete record of what was repaired and permitted.

faqs.q: Do you winterize vacant Fort Worth homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services winterizes plumbing on vacant homes by draining supply lines, protecting traps and shutting off water service. On pier-and-beam houses, we can also insulate exposed crawlspace lines and repair skirting. After a freeze, we inspect previously winterized homes and document their condition so servicers know right away whether repairs are needed before the next showing. A quick check after each hard freeze is cheap compared with finding a flooded subfloor later.

faqs.q: Will you repair foundations on bank-owned Fort Worth homes?
faqs.a: Yes. A licensed foundation company evaluates the house, and on homes with significant movement an engineer specifies the repair. For a pier-and-beam house that usually means re-leveling and new piers, while a slab ranch may need piers along one settled side. Reports and any transferable warranty are handed over with the file, giving the eventual buyer and their FHA or VA appraiser something concrete to rely on.

faqs.q: Do you cover REO properties across Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Yes. Licensed contractors in our network work throughout Fort Worth as well as Arlington, Haltom City, White Settlement, Benbrook, Richland Hills and Saginaw. Every address is assigned its own field manager, who confirms the correct permit office and code department before work begins. Photo reports, draw requests and lien waivers follow one format for the whole pool, which makes portfolio review faster for asset managers.
